multiobjective-search: multiobjective-search Multi-objective shortest paths: BOA*, BOBA*, EMOA*, NAMOA* and their exact, approximate, anytime and parallel relatives over Pareto frontiers. Given a graph whose edges carry cost vectors (distance and travel time, say, or length, risk and energy), the algorithms find one path for every Pareto-optimal cost vector from a start state to a goal, instead of collapsing the objectives into one weighted sum up front. Every exact search is cross-checked against the others and against a brute-force reference on random graphs with two to four objectives. The crate is no_std with alloc, has no dependencies besides search-core, whose cost and heuristic traits it uses, and ships a loader for the 9th DIMACS Challenge road networks along with the benchmark-suite generators of Peer et al. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Usage Two routes from node 1 to node 3, one shorter and one faster; BOA* returns both: Features - std: links std; no API of its own, required by parallel. - parallel: multi-threaded BOBA* (boba_star_parallel, boba_star_with_parallel), SIP-MOSP (sip_mosp) and parallel MOA* (parallel_moa_star) on std::thread::scope. Algorithms Implemented, cross-checked against each other and against a brute-force reference on random graphs with two to four objectives: - BOA*: bi-objective A* (boa_star) - BOA* with an additive tolerance on the second objective (boa_star_approx) - BOA*ε: BOA* with a multiplicative tolerance 1 + ε on the second objective (boa_star_eps), rational ε = num / den (Epsilon) - A-BOA*ε: anytime approximate bi-objective search (boa_star_anytime), with weighted-sum pruning (boa_star_anytime_ws) and the no-reuse baseline (boa_star_anytime_basic); reports each improved front and its exact factor (ApproxFactor) to a callback and stops on a budget - Iterative-PP-A*: the anytime baseline over PP-A* (pp_a_star_iterative) - A-A*pex, anytime A*pex for any number of objectives (apex_star_anytime, AnytimeApex variants reuse, reuse-enh, restart, hybrid), after Zhang et al. 2024; AnytimeFront takes the objective count - PP-A*: path pairs, tolerances on both objectives (pp_a_star); one-sided bounded test and br returned, so the tolerances never compound - A*pex: approximate search for any number of objectives over apex-path pairs (apex_star), tolerance 1 + ε_i per objective; checked against the paper's Algorithm 2, with its G (default) and L merge methods (MergeRule) - BOBA*: bidirectional bi-objective A* (boba_star) with the paper's four cost-bounded preliminary searches (run one after another), or with caller-supplied heuristics (boba_star_with); with the paper's early solution update and heuristic tuning - Multi-threaded BOBA* behind the parallel feature (boba_star_parallel, boba_star_with_parallel; std::thread::scope, no dependencies), cross-checked against the sequential front - EMOA*: multi-objective A* with truncated dominance checks (emoa_star), sorted Vec instead of a balanced tree - NAMOA*: classic multi-objective A* for admissible heuristics (namoa_star) - NAMOA*dr: NAMOA* with dimensionality reduction (namoa_star_dr) - Multi-valued heuristics (MvHeuristic, SingleValued, mv_heuristic_fn) with NAMOA*dr-mvh (namoa_star_dr_mvh, consistent MVHs) and the lazy L-NAMOA*dr-mvh (namoa_star_dr_mvh_lazy, admissible MVHs), Wolff, Felner, Salzman 2026; width-search: width-search Width-based search (Lipovetzky & Geffner) for planning and search problems: novelty tables, IW(k), iterated width, serialized IW (SIW), BFWS(⟨w_{#g}, #g⟩), BFWS with relaxed-plan counts #r, and Rollout IW(1). These searches need no heuristic: they prune every state that makes no new combination of features true, which bounds IW(k) to O(n^k) expansions for n features, however large the raw state space is. Anything that can enumerate successors and describe states as integer features implements WidthProblem: planning atoms, grid cells, RAM bytes. The sas-plus feature adds an adapter for sas_plus::Task, with goal counts and relaxed plans for BFWS. On the bundled planning fixtures, the expansion counts match LAPKT for IW and stay close for the other searches (see Compared with LAPKT). Usage Implement WidthProblem and run a search. Here, walking from 0 to 5 on a line has width 1: A grid with a key and a door needs width 2, because the agent revisits cells after picking up the key: What "width" means A state's novelty is the size of the smallest set of its features that no earlier state in the search had all at once. A state that reaches a never-seen cell has novelty 1. A state whose cell and key flag were each seen before, but never together, has novelty 2. A state whose every feature combination was seen before has no novelty value; it counts as greater than any k. IW(k) is breadth-first search that drops every non-goal state with novelty greater than k. Goal states are always kept. So it remembers only feature combinations of size up to k, and with n features there are at most O(n^k) of those. A problem's width is, roughly, the smallest k for which IW(k) finds a shortest plan. Formally (Lipovetzky & Geffner, 2012), it is the smallest k such that a chain of feature sets of size at most k leads from the initial state to the goal. Each set in the chain is reached optimally by extending an optimal plan for the previous set by one action. Intuitively, width counts how many facts you must track *jointly* to avoid losing your way: - Walking a line or reaching a cell on an open grid has width 1. Position alone tells you whether a state is new. - The key_door example has width 2. After taking the key, the agent walks back over cells it has visited. Position alone calls those states old and IW(1) prunes them. The pair (cell, has key) shows they are new. Width is a property of the problem *and* of the features you choose. Better features can lower it. Many puzzle and planning domains have width 1 or 2 for a single goal fact, which is why low-k searches go so far. Conjunctive goals ("collect every key") usually have higher width, which is the case BFWS handles by also counting satisfied goals (#g). IW(k) already finds a shortest plan when the problem's *set width* is at most k (Bonet & Geffner, 2024), which can be smaller than the chain-based width above. The crate does not compute a problem's width, and cannot do so cheaply: Nguyen (2026) shows that certifying width at most k is coNP-complete even when the unique optimal plan is known, and that no polynomial-time estimate comes within a factor o(N) for N atoms unless P = NP. Iterated width, which tries k = 1, 2, … in turn, is the practical way to find a k that suffices. How it compares Classic searches rank states by distance: the cost so far (BFS, Dijkstra), plus an estimate of the cost to go (A*). Width-based search ranks them by novelty instead. A state is worth keeping only if it makes some feature value, or some combination of up to k feature values, true for the first time. You don't need a heuristic or a distance metric. You only need features, and the search explores "new things" first. Pros - No heuristic to design. Features (atoms, cell positions, inventory flags, RAM bytes) are usually easy to write down. - Bounded effort. IW(k) expands at most O(n^k) states however big the raw state space is, so it is predictable on combinatorial spaces where BFS blows up. - Many benchmark and puzzle domains have width 1 or 2 per goal atom, so IW(1) and IW(2) solve them quickly. - It works on black-box simulators: it never inspects the transition model, only the features of the states it generates. Cons - IW(k) is incomplete when the problem's width exceeds k. It prunes the state that leads to the goal and reports failure. iterated_width retries with larger k, at a cost that grows steeply with k. - It ignores action costs. Use Dijkstra or A* when you need the cheapest path on a weighted graph. - Results depend on your features. Coarse features prune too much, and redundant ones waste effort. - It is not built for adversarial or stochastic settings. Use minimax or MCTS there. In games Good fits: - Puzzle and level validation. Check that a generated level is solvable (keys, doors, switches, block pushing) and get a witness plan. - Goal-oriented NPC planning (GOAP-style). Features are world-state facts, and you don't need a hand-tuned heuristic per goal. - Automated playtesting on a simulator. Width-based search plays Atari games from the emulator RAM bytes alone (Lipovetzky, Ramirez & Geffner, IJCAI 2015). - Exploration bots. Novelty pruning visits new rooms, items and states before it revisits old ones. Poor fits: - Shortest paths on a weighted grid or navmesh. A* is faster and optimal there (or JPS on uniform-cost grids). - Opponent moves, chance, or continuous physics without a discrete feature encoding. Features - sas-plus: sas::SasProblem, an adapter that runs width-based search on a sas_plus::Task, with goal counts and relaxed plans for BFWS. Tested: end to end on a Fast Downward output.sas (gripper: IW needs width 3 for the conjunctive goal, finding the optimal 5-step plan). Also: IW with k = #variables is complete and optimal on unit-cost random tasks; plans of every search are validated on random tasks, and both BFWS variants find one exactly when the task is solvable. Searches - iw(problem, k) and iterated_width(problem, max_k): IW(k), and IW(1), IW(2), ... until one succeeds. - siw(problem, max_k): a simplified serialized IW. Runs iterated width from the current state until #g drops, appends that subplan, and repeats. LAPKT's SIW tracks goal atoms instead: it keeps every achieved goal, and accepts a new one only if the full goal stays reachable without deleting achieved goals. This version accepts any drop in #g, so its plans can be longer. SIW is fast when goals can be reached one at a time. It gives up when no subgoal is reachable within max_k, either in a dead end left by an earlier subplan or because the next subgoal needs more width. - bfws(problem, k): BFWS(⟨w_{#g}, #g⟩). Novelty is computed per value of #g. - bfws_r(problem, k): BFWS(⟨w_{#g,#r}, #g⟩), LAPKT's BFWS-f5. #r counts how many facts of a relaxed plan the path to a state has reached. The relaxed plan is recomputed at every state where #g drops. Implement RelaxedPlan to use it; SasProblem does, with h_add best supporters. - rollout_iw(problem, seed): Rollout IW(1) (Bandres, Bonet & Geffner, AAAI 2018). It runs depth-first rollouts and prunes a node unless it reaches some feature at a smaller depth than before. The paper uses it to pick actions within a time budget. This version runs until it finds a goal or the root is solved. It reaches every width-1 goal, but its plans need not be shortest. Compared with LAPKT Nodes expanded on the test fixtures, this crate / LAPKT 0.2.1 (Tarski grounder). The searches after IW(1) use width bound 2, the LAPKT default: LAPKT planners: IW_Planner --iw_bound 1 and --iw_bound 2 (the latter runs IW(1), then IW(2)), SIW_Planner, and BFWS with --search_type BFWS-goalcount-only and BFWS-f5. scripts/lapkt-compare.sh reruns them, and tests/it/lapkt_counts.rs pins this crate's side. IW agrees almost exactly, although LAPKT computes novelty over STRIPS atoms and this crate over Fast Downward facts. The other searches differ for three reasons. LAPKT's SIW keeps achieved goals and rejects goals whose achievement would block the rest, so it finds 3- and 7-step plans on sussman-anomaly and bw-large-a where this crate's finds 5 and 14. Tie-breaking differs: LAPKT breaks ties by path cost, this crate by generation order. And LAPKT's relaxed plans come from its own heuristic code, so #r counts different facts. LAPKT reports pruned nodes separately; its generated count plus pruned count is close to this crate's generated. References: Lipovetzky & Geffner, ECAI 2012 and AAAI 2017; Lipovetzky, Ramirez & Geffner, IJCAI 2015; Bandres, Bonet & Geffner, AAAI 2018.
decoupled-search: decoupled-search Decoupled (star-topology) search for factored planning tasks in sas-plus's SAS+ representation, after Gnad and Hoffmann (ICAPS 2015, AIJ 2018). A factoring splits the variables into a center and several leaves; the search then follows paths of global actions only and keeps, per leaf, the cheapest price of every leaf state reachable along the current path. On tasks with loosely coupled components (logistics-style packages around a shared vehicle, independent machines around a common resource), that removes the interleavings of leaf moves which blow up an explicit state space, and the search still returns an ordinary sequential plan for the original task. The crate covers the factoring strategies, cost-optimal (uniform-cost, A*, anytime A*) and satisficing (GBFS) search, the dominance pruning of Torralba, Gnad, Dubbert and Hoffmann (2016) and decoupled heuristics, with plan reconstruction and an independent plan validator. It is no_std with alloc, with and without the optional features except symbolic-leaves, which needs std. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Scope More detail, including how each rule maps to the papers, is in docs/design.md. - Factorings: fork, inverted fork, X-shape, and the incident-arcs and independent-set (maximum leaves) strict-star strategies of Gnad, Poser and Hoffmann (IJCAI 2017), the generalized factorings of Gnad, Torralba and Fišer (ICAPS 2022) with directly interacting leaves and a possibly empty center, explicit partitions, and a strict-star check. Factoring::score reports leaves, mobile leaves, the leaf-action share and leaf sizes; Factoring::auto picks the best-scored strategy with at least two mobile leaves and otherwise falls back to explicit search; Factoring::auto_by_sample picks by short sample searches instead (the paper's selection, with an expansion budget instead of a clock). - Leaf reachability with prices (cheapest cost per leaf state along the center path); stored states keep only reached leaf states, as u16 ranks with u64 prices (no prices at all when all are 0). - Uniform-cost search, A* and anytime A* (Gnad and Hoffmann's Anytime Fork-Root A*, cost-optimal), and GBFS (satisficing), with Config choosing the dominance criterion: basic, frontier, effective prices, leaf simulation, or effective prices over simulation (Torralba, Gnad, Dubbert and Hoffmann 2016, generalised to global actions that touch leaves), optionally with one g budget shared by all leaves; the default switches to simulation only once the search has spent its cost. Optional simulation-based leaf reduction (Config::reduce_leaves, the superfluous-transition rule of the paper's technical report with a removal order that keeps it sound), and Config::reduced_task without the operators it makes useless, for heuristics. Search statistics come with every Outcome. - Optional partial-order reduction (Config::stubborn_sets): the decoupled strong stubborn sets of Gnad, Hoffmann and Wehrle (JAIR 2019) for general star factorings. The paper proves they keep optimality and completeness under duplicate detection; the combinations with dominance pruning and leaf reduction that its proof does not cover are listed in the stubborn_sets documentation. - Optional symbolic leaves (Config::symbolic_leaves, feature symbolic-leaves): leaf pricing functions as BDDs (Gnad, Torralba and Hoffmann, SoCS 2017) for leaves too large to enumerate, with small leaves kept enumerated next to them. Same state space and results as explicit leaves, under basic dominance. Optionally a symbolic center (Config::symbolic_center): one search node per set of center states that share their leaf pricing and cost. - Reachability-only leaves (no prices) for GBFS. - Conditional effects on a leaf conditioned on the center and that leaf, on the center conditioned on the center; derived variables that depend on the center and at most one leaf. Everything else is rejected with a precise error. - Heuristics on decoupled states: h^max (admissible) and h^FF, both seeded with per-fact leaf prices (FactPrices, constructible for tests), with the merge-and-shrink feature an admissible merge-and-shrink adapter (MasHeuristic), and with the lm-cut feature an admissible LM-cut adapter (LmCutHeuristic, from planning-heuristics). - Reconstruction of a sequential plan for the original task, and Plan::validate. Usage Features - merge-and-shrink: MasHeuristic, an admissible merge-and-shrink heuristic on decoupled states, from merge-and-shrink. - lm-cut: LmCutHeuristic, an admissible LM-cut heuristic on decoupled states, from planning-heuristics. - symbolic-leaves: Config::symbolic_leaves, leaf pricing functions as BDDs, and Config::symbolic_center, search nodes that hold sets of center states, both on symbolic-search. Needs std. The crate is no_std with alloc, with and without the features, except symbolic-leaves.
symbolic-search: symbolic-search Symbolic state-space search for SAS+ planning tasks from sas-plus, with binary decision diagrams (BDDs) as the state-set representation. Instead of expanding one state at a time, every search step maps a whole layer of states through the operators' transition relations at once, which is what makes symbolic search strong on cost-optimal planning tasks with large, regular state spaces. The crate implements symbolic BFS and Dijkstra (forward, backward and bidirectional), BDDA* and greedy best-first search with symbolic abstraction heuristics, and SymBA* (the bidirectional A* with perimeter abstractions of Torralba et al.), and every search returns a reconstructed plan with its cost. BDDs come from oxidd behind a sealed backend trait; a small plain-Rust reference BDD implements the same trait and is used to cross-check oxidd in the tests. Node tables are sized from the task and grow on demand, so a search that runs out of nodes retries with a larger table instead of failing. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Scope - Binary encoding of sas_plus::Task states with a Gamer-style static variable order. - Per-operator transition relations (with conditional effects), merged per cost into disjunctive groups up to a node limit, or split into per-variable conjunctive clusters with early quantification (greedy or IWLS95 schedule). - Symbolic forward and backward BFS (unit cost). - Symbolic Dijkstra forward, backward and bidirectional (action costs, zero costs included). - BDDA* and symbolic greedy best-first search with heuristics stored as one BDD per h value, from symbolic pattern databases, canonical PDB collections (maximum over additive subsets, capped), symbolic merge-and-shrink (linear merging, h-preserving node-limited shrinking) or explicit estimates. - SymBA*: bidirectional A* with perimeter abstractions that drop variables or single bits (value merging), or merge-and-shrink perimeters, resumable abstract searches per direction, separate concrete and abstract node limits, and an expansion and time budget (SymbaConfig). An exhausted budget reports the best plan found so far and a lower bound. - Config::for_task sizes the node table from the task; running out of nodes retries with a larger table up to Config::max_node_capacity. - The BDD library sits behind the sealed backend::Backend trait; SymbolicTask::with_backend also runs on backend::ReferenceBdd.
miniplan: miniplan A PDDL planner library built around the pddl crate. miniplan is a grounded, classical PDDL planner that you can use as a Rust library or as the miniplan command-line tool. It reads PDDL with the pddl crate, grounds the task into a compact bitset representation and searches it with breadth-first search, A*, greedy best-first search or one of four bidirectional searches (bidirectional Dijkstra and BFS, NBS and BAE*), guided by h^FF, h^add, h^max or the goal count. It handles STRIPS with typing, negative preconditions, conditional effects, disjunctive preconditions and derived predicates, and writes plans as plain text, in IPC format or as JSON. The CLI also has an interactive terminal UI for trying planners on a problem. Features - PDDL 3.x parsing via pddl-rs - Grounding to a compact bitset-based internal representation - Planners: - bfs — blind breadth-first search (optimal) - astar — A* with pluggable heuristics (optimal) - gbfs — greedy best-first search (fast, non-optimal) - bidij — bidirectional Dijkstra (cost-aware, optimal) - bibfs-uc — bidirectional BFS (uniform-cost, optimal) - nbs — Near-Optimal Bidirectional Search (heuristic-guided, non-optimal with HFF) - bae — Bidirectional A* with Error / BAE* (heuristic-guided, non-optimal with HFF) - Bidirectional heuristic search: bidij, bibfs-uc, nbs (NBS), bae (BAE*) - Heuristics: hff (relaxed-plan), hadd, hmax, goal-count, blind - Output formats: plain, IPC, JSON - Search limits: time budget, node budget - Structured logging via tracing - Interactive terminal UI (miniplan tui) for picking a problem, tuning the solver and viewing the plan Quick Start (CLI) Solve a bundled example with search statistics: Parse and ground a problem without solving: List available planners and heuristics: CLI Reference Commands solve Flags Exit Codes Library Usage See docs.rs for the full API. planning-heuristics: planning-heuristics Goal-distance heuristics for classical planning tasks in sas-plus's finite-domain representation: the delete-relaxation family (h_max, h_add, h_FF, h_sa, h²), red-black planning, landmarks with count, uniform and optimal cost partitioning, LM-cut, operator counting and adapters for abstraction heuristics. The crate is no_std with alloc (only the LP-based heuristics behind the lp feature need std), and every state heuristic implements search-core's Heuristic trait, so it plugs into any search crate built on it. The admissible heuristics (h_max, LM-cut, landmark cost partitioning, h², operator counting, abstractions) are tested against exact goal distances computed by brute force. One shared Relaxation is Sync, so a parallel search can build it once and hand each thread its own heuristic. merge-and-shrink: merge-and-shrink Merge-and-shrink abstraction heuristics for factored transition systems, in no_std Rust (with alloc) and without unsafe code: atomic factors, synchronized products, linear, DFP and SCC-DFP merge strategies, exact label reduction, pruning of unreachable and dead states, and exact, greedy and size-bounded goal-respecting bisimulation. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Optimal planners such as A* need a heuristic that never overestimates the cost to the goal. Abstraction heuristics get one by mapping the huge concrete state space onto a much smaller abstract one, computing exact goal distances there, and using those distances as lower bounds. Merge-and-shrink builds such abstractions over *all* variables of a task at once, so it can capture interactions between variables that pattern databases, which project onto a few variables, cannot see. The crate turns a SAS+ task (for example Fast Downward translator output, read through sas-plus) into a heuristic you can query per state: value returns the estimated cost, or None when the state is a proven dead end or was pruned as unreachable from the initial state. Because the heuristic also implements sas_plus::Abstraction, it plugs into cost-partition, which adds up several abstraction heuristics admissibly. How it works 1. Atomic factors. Each variable becomes a small transition system over its values. Its labels are the task's operators. 2. Pick. A merge strategy picks the next two factors. LinearMerge merges the variables in a fixed order. Dfp picks the pair whose shared operators lead closest to the goal. SccDfp first merges the variables of each strongly connected component of the causal graph, then continues with Dfp. 3. Reduce labels. Operators of equal cost that only one factor can tell apart are combined into one label in every factor. This is exact and lets bisimulation group more states. The final abstraction is labeled with operator ids again. 4. Shrink. Both factors are shrunk so that their product fits max_states. A shrink strategy groups states that behave alike. Bisimulation starts from groups of states with the same goal distance and goal status, and splits them until all states in a group can reach the same groups by the same labels, which keeps every goal distance exact while often shrinking the factor a lot. At the size limit it stops splitting, closest to the goal first. GreedyBisimulation only looks at transitions on optimal paths, so it shrinks more but is no longer perfect after further merges. NoShrink keeps every state and ignores the limit. 5. Merge and prune. The two factors are replaced by their synchronized product: an operator moves both components at once, so the product tracks both variables together. States that are unreachable from the initial state, or that cannot reach a goal, are dropped. 6. Evaluate. After the last merge, the goal distances of the single remaining factor are the heuristic. A merge tree of lookup tables maps each concrete state to its abstract state, one table per merge, so evaluating a state is cheap. On plain SAS+ tasks, exact bisimulation without a size limit makes the heuristic perfect: it equals the optimal cost on every state without pruning, and on every reachable state with pruning (MergeAndShrink::new prunes by default; pruned states evaluate to None). Conditional effects and derived variables (axioms) are over-approximated by the atomic factors, so there the heuristic stays admissible but can be lower. Usage Build the heuristic for a task from Fast Downward's translator and evaluate it: None from value means a dead end: no plan exists from that state. With pruning (the default), states unreachable from the task's initial state also evaluate to None, even goal states, so build with prune: false to evaluate states from another start. Features no_std (needs alloc). The crate has no Cargo features. It depends on sas-plus 0.2 without its default features. References Helmert, Haslum, Hoffmann & Nissim (JACM 2014); Nissim, Hoffmann & Helmert (IJCAI 2011, greedy bisimulation); Sievers, Wehrle & Helmert (AAAI 2014, label reduction; IJCAI 2016, SCC-DFP); Dräger, Finkbeiner & Podelski (SPIN 2006, DFP); Sievers & Helmert (JAIR 2021).
cost-partition: cost-partition Cost partitioning over *any* sas_plus::Abstraction (projections, merge-and-shrink, ...): saturated cost partitioning for a given order, and the maximum over several orders. Different kinds of abstractions can share one order as Vec. Splitting each operator's cost among several abstractions, so that the parts sum to at most the original cost, makes the *sum* of their heuristics admissible. The crate implements saturated cost partitioning after Seipp, Keller & Helmert (JAIR 2020) and its maximum over orders, is no_std with alloc, and is checked against exact goal distances on random tasks and real translator output. What cost partitioning is A planning heuristic estimates, for a state, the cost of the cheapest plan to a goal. Optimal search such as A* needs it to be *admissible*: it never estimates more than the true optimum h*. An *abstraction* gives such a heuristic cheaply. It maps every state to a smaller abstract state space, for example a projection that keeps only some variables, and uses the goal distance there as the estimate. Each abstraction is admissible on its own, but usually weak, because it sees only part of the task. Adding the estimates of several abstractions is not admissible in general. Each one charges the full cost of every operator it needs, so an operator that several abstractions need is paid for several times. On the translated gripper-4 task, the projections' estimates add up to 24, while the optimal plan costs 9. Cost partitioning removes the double counting. Each operator's cost is split into shares, one per abstraction, so that the shares sum to at most the original cost. Each abstraction then computes its goal distances under its own shares only. Any plan pays every operator at most once in total across the abstractions, so the sum of their estimates is admissible again. How saturated cost partitioning works Saturated cost partitioning (SCP) builds the shares greedily, one abstraction at a time, in a given order: 1. Compute the abstraction's goal distances under the costs that are still left. 2. Take its *saturated* cost function: for each operator, the least cost that keeps all of those goal distances. That is the largest drop in goal distance along any transition the operator labels. Operators that do not bring this abstraction closer to the goal get 0. 3. Subtract the saturated costs from what is left, and pass the rest on to the next abstraction. An abstraction early in the order keeps its full estimate and takes only the costs it needs, so later abstractions still get the costs it has no use for. Abstractions left out of the order get no costs, but still report dead ends: states from which no plan exists. A small example: operators a (cost 2) and b (cost 3), with the optimal plan a, b, so h* = 5. Abstraction X only notices a, and abstraction Y notices both. Different orders give different estimates, and none is best for every state. MaxOverOrders computes SCP for several orders and takes the largest estimate, which is still admissible. Usage Build projections of a task from Fast Downward's translator, partition the costs among them, and evaluate the heuristic: None from value means a dead end: no plan exists from that state. Examples Both are meant for small tasks. They run on the translated gripper-4 task from this repository by default, or on the translator output passed as an argument. task examples runs both (task examples -- path/to/output.sas for another task). heuristics shows why costs are partitioned. Adding the projections' estimates with full costs overestimates the optimum, so the sum is not admissible. SCP splits the costs first: it stays admissible and is stronger than the best single projection. Its estimates for gripper-4: astar solves the task optimally with A*, blind and guided by SCP, and prints the plan. Both plans are optimal; the guided search expands fewer states. Its summary for gripper-4, before the plan: Features no_std (needs alloc). The crate has no Cargo features. It depends on sas-plus without its default features.
mapf-search: mapf-search Multi-agent pathfinding: CBS, CBS-TA, ECBS, ICTS, PBS, PIBT (also for agents that need time to turn), M*, EPEA*, MAPF-LNS2 and multi-objective MO-CBS on grids and general graphs. Given a graph and a set of agents with start and goal vertices, the solvers find one path per agent so that no two agents ever share a vertex or swap along an edge. CBS, ICTS, M* and EPEA* minimize the sum of costs or the makespan, ECBS stays within a given factor of the optimum, and PBS, PIBT and MAPF-LNS2 trade optimality for speed. CBS-TA also picks the goals: each agent gets one of its candidate goals, optimally over all assignments. The optimal solvers are checked against a joint-space oracle by property tests, and M* and EPEA* also prove when an instance has no solution. The crate is no_std with alloc, uses the A* of heuristic-search as its single-agent low level, and reads the Moving AI .map and .scen benchmark formats. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Algorithms - CBS, optimal for sum of costs or makespan, with prioritized (cardinal) conflicts, bypass, the CG, DG and WDG heuristics, a conflict avoidance table and disjoint splitting (with positive constraints), each switchable (cbs, cbs_with, CbsConfig) - CBS-TA, conflict-based search with task assignment: each agent has candidate goals, and the plan is optimal over all assignments, for sum of costs or makespan (cbs_ta, cbs_ta_with, TaskInstance) - FOCBS, flow-oracle CBS for agents without goals (idle robots that only have to get out of the way): CBS over the agents with goals, a min-cost flow routes the idle ones, and the flow's minimum cut tells CBS which reservations block them; optimal sum of costs for the agents with goals, fewest moves for the idle ones given those paths (focbs, focbs_with, UaInstance) - ECBS, bounded-suboptimal, focal search at both levels (ecbs) - PBS, priority-based search: fast, neither optimal nor complete (pbs) - PIBT, priority inheritance with backtracking: plans one time step for all agents at a time, very fast, neither optimal nor complete (pibt) - PIBT*_T, PIBT for robots that face a heading, move only forward and need time to turn in place, with cycle handling, swaps and a push escape trigger, on grids or any OrientedGraph; task-allocation: task-allocation Decentralized multi-agent task allocation in Rust: agents decide among themselves who does which task, exchanging bids whenever they can communicate, without a central authority. Scope - Consensus-based bundle algorithm (CBBA) and its variants, converging to conflict-free assignments under delayed and intermittent communication - Coupled-constraint CBBA for tasks that depend on or exclude each other, and that must start within limits of each other - Sequential and combinatorial auctions as baselines - Task scores from user-supplied costs, such as travel time, deadlines or resource use - A deterministic simulated network (seeded delays, losses and partitions) to test teams on - Timed routes: a ready-made path score from travel times, service windows and rewards that decay with the finish time - Greedy bundle construction from marginal gains, with a check for diminishing gains - Centralized references: the sequential greedy assignment, and the exhaustive optimum for small instances Usage A valuation scores what a task is worth to one agent, given the tasks it already holds. Agents bid with these scores, so a task that does not fit, such as one that would miss its deadline, scores None and gets no bid. Here, a rover works through its bundle one task after another. Allocation algorithms work on task identifiers. Each agent's valuation looks up what it needs, and an algorithm returns one bundle per agent. Here, two rovers on a line split three sites, each going for what is closest to its last stop: Decentralized, each rover runs a CBBA agent and exchanges messages with whoever it can reach. The simulated network here loses a third of all messages and delays the rest by up to four ticks; the rovers still agree on who does what: On real hardware, call build_bundle and message on every round and pass each message that arrives to receive. Agents created with .with_replan(Replan::Full) rebuild their bundles from scratch every round, which costs more computation, and settle on a sequential greedy assignment: the centralized one, up to the order in which tied gains are resolved. The crate is no_std, needs alloc, and has no runtime dependencies. Examples Each example pairs the allocation with a sibling crate, without making it a dependency of this one: - warehouse_grid: robots on a floor plan, with travel times from A* in heuristic-search, agreeing over a lossy network. - relay_timing: rovers' plans checked against a handoff between them as a simple temporal network in temporal-control, and reallocated with a tighter deadline when they miss it. - drone_battery: each drone's battery reserve checked inside its valuation with resource-timeline, and a shared uplink checked across all drones afterwards. - field_rrt: travel around an obstacle from RRT* in sampling-planning, comparing CBBA with the auctions, sequential greedy and the optimum. Run one with cargo run --release --example warehouse_grid.
stochastic-search: stochastic-search Planning under probabilistic outcomes: LAO*, iLAO*, CG-iLAO*, RTDP, LRTDP, BRTDP, FRTDP, VPI-RTDP, POMCP, DESPOT, and the multi-objective MOLAO*, iMOLAO* and MOLRTDP. When actions have uncertain outcomes (a wheel slips, a request times out), a single path is no longer a plan: the crate solves stochastic shortest path problems (SSPs) and returns a value function with a greedy policy that says what to do in every state the plan can reach. Problems are described through a small Mdp trait with callbacks, so states are generated on demand rather than enumerated up front; dead ends can be treated as infinitely or finitely expensive. Partially observable problems use a separate generative POMDP model with the online planners POMCP and DESPOT, and problems with several cost dimensions get the multi-objective algorithms of Chen, Trevizan and Thiébaux. The crate is no_std with alloc, and value iteration serves as the reference that the other algorithms are tested against. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Scope - Value iteration, RTDP, labeled RTDP (LRTDP), classic LAO*, iLAO* and CG-iLAO* for stochastic shortest path problems, with infinite or finite-penalty dead ends - Bounded RTDP (BRTDP), focused RTDP (FRTDP) and VPI-RTDP with lower and upper bounds and an upper-greedy policy; upper bounds must be finite, so infinite dead ends need a lower bound that proves them (or use a penalty) - A generative POMDP model with online planners POMCP and anytime regularized DESPOT (Ye et al. 2017) over particle beliefs, with tree reuse between decisions, a particle filter with reinvigoration, POMCP exploration calibration, progress events and dedicated tree counters - Multi-objective SSPs (MoMdp, cost vectors) with the algorithms of Chen, Trevizan and Thiébaux (2023): MOLAO*, iMOLAO* and MOLRTDP, with multi-objective value iteration as the reference. They return the convex coverage set of deterministic proper policies under the weak improper policy assumption (bound b). Heuristics: blind, ideal point of single-objective heuristics, and MOVI on an abstraction or on the all-outcomes determinisation. The paper's factored heuristics (h^max, comax, PDBs) are not implemented, because the crate has no factored model - Shared traits: Goal, Heuristic, heuristic_fn and Budget come from search-core and are re-exported here; Budget bounds are Budget. Zero is search-core's as well (it covers f64); the multi-objective algorithms use the local ZeroVector. See docs/design.md for the model and its guarantees. game-tree-search: game-tree-search Adversarial game-tree search in Rust for computer opponents in board, card and turn-based games: choosing a move when an opponent chooses the next one. Scope - Minimax and negamax - Alpha-beta pruning with move ordering, principal variation search (PVS/NegaScout) and MTD(f) - Iterative deepening with transposition tables, aspiration windows and quiescence search - Expectimax for games with chance nodes - Monte Carlo tree search with UCT Single-agent search, including iterative deepening (IDDFS, IDA*), lives in heuristic-search. Usage A game describes its positions, the moves available in them, which side is to move and how good a position is for the maximizing side. The side to move belongs to the position, so one side may move several times in a row. Here, one-pile Nim: players take one or two stones, and whoever cannot move has lost. The crate is no_std and needs alloc. Its required dependencies are search-core, for the shared Budget trait, and libm, for the square roots and logarithms of Monte Carlo tree search. Many searches at once Game AI often runs a search per unit or agent, every frame. Keep one Searcher (or Mcts) per thread or agent and pass the game by reference: every search takes &G and never mutates it, so a Sync game is shared between threads as it is, and a searcher is Send whenever its moves and scores are. A warm searcher reuses its buffers, so a search allocates only the result it returns. Give each agent its own transposition table, or none; with the parallel feature, a SharedTable serves several threads at once. Features - hashbrown: MapTable, a transposition table backed by a hashbrown hash map. Without it, the fixed-size SlotTable is available. - rand_core: RandCore, so Monte Carlo tree search can draw from any rand_core 0.10 generator instead of its built-in, seeded SplitMix64. - parallel: searches on std threads. Mcts::search_parallel runs root-parallel Monte Carlo tree search, one tree per thread with their root statistics added up; deepen_shared runs Lazy SMP, several deepening threads sharing one SharedTable. Every feature combination except parallel stays no_std; parallel needs std for its threads.
constraint-search: constraint-search Finite-domain constraint satisfaction in Rust: variables with small domains, constraints that prune them, and search for the assignments that remain. Scope - Finite-domain variables with bitset domains and a trail for undoing changes on backtrack - Propagators run to a fixpoint, including all-different with complete Hall-set reasoning, constraints given by their allowed tuples, weighted sums and nonogram lines - Pluggable inference rules ordered by cost, for human-style solving, hints, explanations and difficulty grading - Backtracking search with variable and value ordering heuristics under a budget, resumable so the work can be spread across frames or ticks - Solution counting with early stop, for checking that a puzzle has a unique solution - Problems with many solutions: the values certain in every solution (backbone), each value's probability (marginals), and random solutions to sample hidden information - Exact cover with dancing links Typical uses are logic puzzles (Sudoku and its variants, nonograms, KenKen, Kakuro, logic grids, cryptarithms), Minesweeper and card-location deduction, map colouring, timetabling and small scheduling problems. Usage A Model holds the variables and constraints and can be shared between threads. A Solver borrows it and reuses its working state from one search to the next. Here, the 3×3 Latin squares: every row and column holds the values 0, 1 and 2 once. Custom constraints implement Propagator; Table lists allowed tuples for small ones, and Linear and Line cover sums and nonogram clues. For human-style solving, Rules applies costed techniques (VariableSubset, ValueSubset, GroupIntersection or your own Rule), cheapest first. Each step can serve as a hint, and the most expensive rule a solve needed grades the puzzle. robust-planning: robust-planning Motion planning that proves its edges safe: planners whose nodes carry reachable sets (sparse polynomial zonotopes from polyzonotope) instead of single states, so a path is accepted only when every state the system can reach under bounded disturbances and initial uncertainty stays clear of the obstacles. The crate has Robust-RRT, Robust RRT* and a reachability-guided A* over motion primitives, plus an adapter that lets the planners of sampling-planning check their edges the same way. Every check is conservative: a check that cannot prove safety returns Indeterminate, never Safe, and planners reject it. With the sound feature, polyzonotope rounds outward and a Safe verdict becomes a proof rather than "safe up to floating-point rounding". Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Features - Robust-RRT: an RRT whose nodes carry reachable sets (RobustRrt). - Robust RRT*: choose-parent and rewiring over proven-safe edges only; a rewire re-propagates and re-proves the whole moved subtree and commits only if all of it stays proven safe and no goal node loses the goal, within a per-iteration budget (RobustRrtStar). - Reachability-guided search: A* over reachable-set nodes along motion primitives, with lattice deduplication, optional workspace bounds on nominal states or whole sets, a goal radius derived from the goal, opt-in pruning of superseded subtrees, and opt-in proven set-in-set deduplication for zonotopes in up to four dimensions (ReachSearch, decide_within). - A robustness-weighted cost (Cost::WidthWeighted) for RobustRrtStar and ReachSearch. - Edge checks for sampling-planning planners in Euclidean spaces (ReachChecker). - Pluggable steering (Steer, WithSteering), goals (Goal, PolytopeGoal) and certified collision witnesses (Reach::certify_collision). - Polytope obstacles checked against reachable sets, with optional refinement by splitting (Obstacles). - Dynamics models on polyzonotope-reach, behind the reach feature: validated continuous-time reachable sets of linear (models::Linear) and nonlinear (models::Nonlinear) systems. Their cover sets enclose the motion between time steps. Usage See the crate documentation and docs/design.md for the safety semantics. The example plans through a 2D world with an affine model, and the benchmarks time the search and Robust RRT*:

Every objective is minimised, all randomness comes from a caller-provided rand_core::Rng (the crate ships SplitMix64), and every run takes a budget that is asked before each evaluation, so seeded runs are reproducible and limits are exact. CMA-ES follows Hansen's tutorial exactly and is tested against its Table 1. See docs/design.md for the architecture, the design rules and the paper table. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Scope Implemented: - Core: operator traits (initialisation, selection, crossover, mutation, repair) with closure adapters and GLEAM-style operator mixes; representations for real vectors (SBX, BLX-α, polynomial, Gaussian, iso+line, Latin hypercube), bit and integer strings, permutations (PMX, OX, CX, ERX, swap, insertion, inversion, scramble) and GLEAM action chains (variable-length, typed, parameterised genes with gene- and chain-level operators); polyzonotope: polyzonotope Sparse polynomial zonotopes (Kochdumper & Althoff, IEEE TAC 2021), zonotopes, and interval boxes, for set-based reachability analysis. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Who this is for - Engineers verifying controllers for drones, vehicles, robot arms or spacecraft, who need to show that every state reachable under bounded noise and parameter uncertainty stays inside a safe region. - Researchers in set-based methods who want sparse polynomial zonotopes, zonotope order reduction and three-valued polytope checks in Rust, without a MATLAB runtime. - Embedded targets: the sets work without std, down to Cortex-M0 with a critical-section implementation. - To propagate sets through linear or nonlinear dynamics over time (flowpipes), use polyzonotope-reach from this workspace, which builds on these types. - To plan paths whose edges are proven safe under uncertainty, robust-planning wraps these sets in Robust-RRT, Robust RRT* and a reachability-guided search; for plain sampling-based planning without uncertainty, sampling-planning. The representation Dependent factors carry global FactorIds, so sets derived from the same uncertainty stay correlated. ConstrainedPolyZonotope (Kochdumper & Althoff 2023) restricts a sparse polynomial zonotope to the factor values where a polynomial constraint vanishes: "Exact" means exact in real arithmetic. In f64 the coefficients are rounded, unless you enable the sound feature (below). Checking sets against obstacles A Polytope is an intersection of Halfspaces { x | aᵀx <= d }, and Polytope::from_box turns an IntervalBox into one. intersection answers whether a set meets a polytope, containment whether it lies inside. Both return three values, because an enclosure can prove a negative but not a positive: - Intersection::Disjoint and Containment::Inside come from outer bounds, and are proofs. They are rigorous only with the sound feature; in plain f64, rounding can make them wrong by a few ulps at the boundary. - Intersection::Intersects and Containment::NotInside rest on a witness point, evaluated in plain f64. Near the boundary they are not certified. - Unknown means the split budget ran out, or the remaining piece has nothing left to split. Where safety is at stake, accept only the proofs. Both checks split the set (max_splits in total) until they can decide. A zonotope against a single halfspace needs no splits. Points inside a zonotope, and one zonotope inside another, need linear programming and are not covered. Usage The parabola arc { (α, α²) | α ∈ -1, 1 } is a curved set that no zonotope represents exactly: no_std The crate is no_std with alloc. The default std feature only switches monomial powers to f64::powi; without it, they are computed by repeated squaring: Fresh FactorIds come from a global 64-bit counter in portable-atomic. Targets with 64-bit atomics, and those with 32-bit compare-and-swap such as Cortex-M3/M4, work as they are. Targets without any atomic read-modify-write, such as Cortex-M0 (thumbv6m-none-eabi) or riscv32imc, need portable-atomic's critical-section feature in your own Cargo.toml, plus a critical-section implementation for the chip. Sound mode By default, arithmetic is plain f64. An enclosure can then miss a point by a few ulps, so don't rely on it for formal verification. The sound feature fixes that with outward rounding from inari: - interval_hull and Interval addition round their bounds outward, and Zonotope::from_box rounds its half widths up. - Every operation listed as exact computes its new coefficients in interval arithmetic. It stores their midpoints and adds one axis-aligned generator for each dimension whose rounding error is nonzero: an independent generator for a SparsePolyZonotope, a plain generator for a Zonotope. The result then encloses the set real arithmetic would give. - Every coefficient must be finite. This is a precondition, not a check: a NaN or an infinity panics once the arithmetic touches it, but coefficients an operation only copies pass through unchecked. So under sound, the number of generators can grow after any exact operation, and so can the number of β values that positional evaluate expects. That is up to 2 · dim per call, since exact_plus and split append one batch and their internal compact may append another. Cargo unifies features across the dependency graph, so read the count instead of assuming it: independent_generators().ncols() on a SparsePolyZonotope, num_generators() on a Zonotope. The error generators pile up over long chains of operations. reduce folds them back into a box. inari needs std and runs only on x86-64 (Haswell or newer) and AArch64.
