polyzonotope-reach: polyzonotope-reach Reachable-set over-approximation for dynamical systems, with the sparse polynomial zonotopes of polyzonotope. Given a set of start states and a set of inputs, the crate computes flowpipes: for each time step, one set that holds every state at the end of the step and one that holds every state during it. LinearReach handles x' = A x + B u with a Taylor-series matrix exponential and an enclosed remainder; NonlinearReach handles x' = f(x, u) by conservative linearization or conservative polynomialization, with set splitting, merging and adaptive steps. A step it cannot prove is refused rather than returned, and with the sound feature the floating-point rounding is enclosed as well. The crate is no_std with alloc. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Linear systems LinearReach propagates x' = A x + B u, where the input u(t) can be any integrable signal with values in a zonotope U. Each step t_k, t_k + r returns two sets: - time_point holds every state at t_k + r: e^{Ar} X ⊕ Γ(r) B c_u ⊕ R_p(B U_Δ). - time_interval holds every state at any t in the step. It is the hull of X and its successor (Girard 2005), plus the curvature corrections F X and F̃ B c_u, plus R_p. The matrix exponential is a truncated Taylor series with its remainder E(r) carried as an interval matrix (Althoff 2010). c_u is the center of U, and R_p bounds the response to the varying part U_Δ. Sets grow by a few generators per step. Call reduce from polyzonotope between steps to keep them small. Nonlinear systems NonlinearReach propagates x' = f(x, u) for any Dynamics: a type that encloses f, its Jacobian and its Hessians over boxes in interval arithmetic, and optionally its third derivatives. Polynomial implements it for polynomial vector fields and derives all of them itself. NonlinearSettings::method picks how each step abstracts f. Conservative linearization Method::Linearization (Althoff, Stursberg & Buss 2008) is the default, since it needs the Hessians only: 1. Linearize at z* = (x*, c_u), where x* is the middle of the set moved half a step along f. This gives x' = A x + B u + w. 2. Run the linear step with the abstraction error as an extra input, bounded by a guessed box Ψ̄. 3. Bound the true error over the time-interval set R(τ) and U. By Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder, it is Δzᵀ Q Δz plus a remainder. Q is the center of ½ H over a box that holds every segment from z* into R(τ) × U. The quadratic part is a polynomial zonotope (quadratic_map), so its hull sees x₀² as non-negative. The spread of the Hessian and of the Jacobian go through intervals. 4. Accept the step if the error lies in Ψ̄. Otherwise widen Ψ̄ and retry. After max_iterations tries, refuse with ReachError::AbstractionDiverged. Conservative polynomialization Method::Polynomialization (Althoff 2013) keeps the second- and third-order error at the start set as a polynomial zonotope over the set's factors. It needs Dynamics::third_derivatives, and refuses with ReachError::MissingDerivatives without them. With s = (x_k − x_m, 0) the start of a trajectory relative to the middle x_m of the set, and δ(t) = Δz(t) − s what changes during the step, the error splits exactly into: - the static part sᵀ Q s + P s³ with Q = ½ H(z*) and P ≈ ⅙ ∂³f(z*). It depends on x_k alone, so it is computed once per step with quadratic_map and cubic_map over the factors of X. It enters as the constant input v of the augmented system x' = A x + v, v' = 0, x₀' = 0, started from { (x_k, ψ_s(x_k), x_k) }, and keeps its dependencies. - the dynamic part: sᵀ (½H) δ + δᵀ (½H) s + δᵀ (½H) δ, the change P (Δz³ − s³) of the cubic term during the step, the Lagrange remainder ⅙ Σ (∂³f(ξ) − 6P) Δz Δz Δz over a box that holds every segment from z*, and the rounding spreads of J(z*) and H(z*). For a field of degree 3 or less, ∂³f is constant and that remainder comes from rounding only. All of it goes through interval arithmetic and into the guessed box Ψ̄. The state part of δ is x(t) − x_k minus the half step, with x(t) − x_k in both the flow box 0, r f(□R(τ) × □U) and the hull of x − x₀ over the time-interval set of the augmented system, which carries a constant copy x₀ = x_k of the start state. In that difference the factors of X cancel, so it does not grow with the set the way the flow box does. The inputs are never static, since u(t) may jump inside U during the step: every term with u − u* is dynamic. The static error triples the degree of the set with each step, so monomials above max_degree (default 4) are enclosed as independent generators. The rustdoc of Method::Polynomialization has the full soundness argument. Keeping dependencies through reduction The linear step and the order reduction make generators independent: the error box, the time-interval hull, and every dependent monomial that reduction encloses. In the next step's quadratic map, products of independent generators are enclosed one by one, so a wide set loses its shape step by step. With Restructure::Lift, every independent generator of the time-point set becomes a dependent factor of its own after the Girard reduction. That is exact, and later quadratic maps then treat those factors as polynomials. Where nothing merges, it costs 1.5 to 1.7 times as much (40 steps of Van der Pol from ρ = 0.5), and gains little since the time-interval hull pairs the independent generators of X with their images: on Van der Pol from ρ = 0.5, polynomialization ends 3% narrower with lifting, and on the damped cubic of the tests 31% wider, with 6 pieces either way. Lifted pieces merge more readily, though: on the damped cubic they merge back to 3 and the run is a third faster. So the default is Restructure::Off, which keeps the generators independent. Adaptive steps NonlinearSettings::adaptive takes an Adaptive with min_step and max_step. When a time step is refused, the whole time step is retried with a step shrink (default ½) times as long, and pieces are split only at min_step. After a time step whose pieces confirmed their error within easy_guesses (default 3) guesses, the next step is grow (default 1.25) times longer. Every Step records its duration, and reach_for runs until the durations add up to a horizon. Each step is sound for whatever length it uses, and refused attempts leave no set behind; the rustdoc of Adaptive has the argument. Shorter steps are not always better. Each step adds a reduction, and on the damped cubic of the tests, steps of 0.05 diverge where steps of 0.1 do not. Growing steps also made Van der Pol's sets wider. So set max_step to the step that works, and let Adaptive shrink only where that step fails. Van der Pol from wide boxes From 1.4, 2.4 ± ρ over 0.8 s, with 12 Taylor terms, order 20 and up to 8 pieces, the width is the sum of the interval-hull widths of the widest time-point piece. "True" is the hull of a 41 × 41 grid of RK4 trajectories. "Proven" is the time up to which the sets are proven. From ρ = 1, neither method gets far: the error box of a set that wide feeds on itself. Shorter steps push the failure out from 0.50 s to 0.68 s with polynomialization, and from 0.26 s to 0.33 s with linearization; the width at 0.16 s is 7.36 against a true 5.34. From ρ = 0.5 with step 0.01, polynomialization's set shrinks after 0.4 s, as the true set does, though at 1.7 times its width. From ρ = 0.2 the two methods end within 9% of each other. Splitting and merging Both sets are reduced to the configured order after every step. reach runs a number of steps and reach_for a duration. A piece that diverges is split in two and retried, up to max_pieces pieces per step. The split cuts the factor of the piece, or the axis of its oriented box, whose halves have the smallest second-order error bound Σ_i |r|ᵀ |H_i| |r|. Factor splits keep the dependencies. The independent generators are boxed and turned into factors first, so that a factor split can reach the bulk of the set. Box splits halve the whole extent along an axis. On Van der Pol and the cubic drift, each kind wins about half of the splits. Splitting::Factors allows factor splits only, which keeps every dependency but needs more pieces: 4 instead of 2 for the cubic drift from radius 0.5 with linearization. After each step, two pieces merge into one when the hull of their merged enclosure is at most merge_tolerance (default 10%) larger by volume than their two hulls together. The merged set is also never wider than half the narrowest piece that has diverged so far. The merge encloses λ a + (1 − λ) b as ½ (a + b) + ν ½ (a − b) with a fresh factor ν. The factors of the two pieces are paired, so two halves of a factor split merge back into their parent exactly. A refusal means that no set was proven for that step. The crate does not hand back a set it could not confirm. reach returns a ReachFailure then, which holds the steps proven before the failing one and the ReachError that stopped it. ReachError is #non_exhaustive. Soundness The over-approximation is sound in real arithmetic. The Taylor remainder, the time-interval corrections and the input response are all enclosed, so the sets are larger than the true reachable set, never smaller. For nonlinear systems, the argument is the usual one for the error check. If the error over R(τ) lies in Ψ̄, no trajectory can leave R(τ) during the step. So the linear model plus an input in Ψ̄ covers every trajectory. Polynomialization bounds x(t) − x_k by the flow over R(τ), which rests on the same hypothesis. Splits are exact, and a merge encloses the convex hull of both pieces. With the sound feature, the rounding of the floating-point computation is covered as well. The series terms, the factorials and the remainder are computed in outward-rounded interval arithmetic, and every set operation tracks its own rounding errors. The nonlinear step evaluates f and its derivatives in interval arithmetic. The model offset and the error terms are also computed that way, so they are rounded outward too. The one exception is the coefficient i^{-i/(i-1)} − i^{-1/(i-1)} of the time-interval correction. It comes from libm::pow, which is not correctly rounded, so it is widened by a relative 1e-12 instead.
temporal-control: temporal-control Simple temporal networks with uncertainty: dynamic controllability checking on the ground and dispatchable execution onboard, down to no_std targets without a heap. A simple temporal network (STN) is a set of time points with "at least a, at most b ticks apart" constraints between them; an STNU adds contingent links, durations that nature picks within known bounds (an activity whose end the system only observes). The crate decides whether such a network can always be executed, whatever the contingent durations turn out to be, and if so compiles it into a dispatchable form that a small fixed-capacity dispatcher executes tick by tick. When a network is not controllable, the answer names the requirements and contingent bounds that conflict. All time values are integer ticks, all arithmetic is checked, and every algorithm runs under an explicit compute and memory budget, so an exhausted budget yields an error rather than a verdict. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Scope - STN consistency (Bellman-Ford) with negative-cycle explanation. - STN minimal network (Floyd-Warshall). - STN minimal constraints of the constrained pairs only (P³C, Planken, de Weerdt and van der Krogt 2008). - Incremental STN consistency, O(n^2) per constraint. - Dispatchable STN by dominated-edge filtering (Muscettola, Morris and Tsamardinos 1998, as restated by Morris 2014; minimal except for edge copies on simultaneous points, if that restatement is complete). - Extended dispatchable STNU: Morris 2014 dispatchable variant, reduced by minDispESTNU (without diamonds). - STNU dynamic controllability: labelled closure with extended dispatchable network (reference), Morris 2014 O(n^3) backpropagation (default checker), RUL⁻ (Cairo, Hunsberger and Rizzi 2018), RUL2021 (Hunsberger and Posenato 2022), and per-label backpropagation (cross-check). - Explanations of non-controllability (semi-reducible negative cycles). - Onboard dispatcher, no_std without alloc, fixed capacity, loaded in place from a const EMPTY, with u16/u32/usize index types for its internal handles. - Compact checksummed encoding (CRC-32) of dispatchable networks, with a no-alloc decoder. - cargo fuzz targets (decoder, dispatcher calls, DC checker agreement, STN algorithm agreement) and Kani harnesses for the dispatcher and the decoder, all verified at small bounds (see section 8 of docs/design.md). - The papers' own examples as tests, and every algorithm compared with its paper (section 12 of the design). Reaction-time semantics: an observation at tick t may trigger executions at the same tick. Next-tick reaction is supported by transforming the network (Stnu::with_reaction). Cargo features Without alloc, the crate offers the Dispatcher, the decoder and their input types, and builds for bare-metal targets such as thumbv7em-none-eabihf (checked in CI).
resource-timeline: resource-timeline Resource timelines for onboard scheduling: energy, memory, thermal and communication budgets. The crate answers one question for a scheduler: if these activities run at these times, does any resource leave its safe range, and if so, when, by how much, and because of whom? A timeline tracks one resource over integer ticks (a battery that drains and charges at given rates, a data buffer, an instrument that can only be claimed once at a time, or a mode that has to hold during an observation), and the check reports the first violation with the activities responsible. On top of that come plans over several timelines, earliest-start search, and envelopes that check a flexible schedule once for every start the windows allow. Every timeline also comes in a fixed-capacity, allocation-free variant for onboard use. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. Scope - Numeric timelines for consumable resources (energy, data volume) with step and rate (piecewise-linear) impacts, and for reusable resources (instruments, transmitters, power channels) with interval claims - State timelines for modes and visibility windows, with set and require impacts - First-violation checks with explanations: the tick, the level or state, and the activities responsible - End-state level targets (for example the battery reserve at the end of a sol) - Incremental add and remove on a sorted change-point profile; level queries at any tick - Profile extraction for display and telemetry: breakpoints, regular samples, and a compact exported profile that answers level queries on its own - Plans over several timelines: atomic placement and earliest-feasible-start search, solved in closed form per linear piece when rates are involved - Fixed-capacity, allocation-free variants of every timeline and of the plan (Fixed, FixedPlan), sharing all logic with the heap variant, with typed capacity errors; the alloc feature (default) adds heap storage, envelopes and the greedy scheduler - A greedy priority scheduler (example and test vehicle), see examples/rover.rs - Level envelopes for activities with start windows: safe, possibly violated or certainly violated for every schedule the windows admit, with uncertain durations (claims and rates anchored at the activity end), precedence constraints (window propagation plus an exact min-cut extreme for stepwise activities), and state envelopes for requirements and conflicts - Precedences between starts and ends (contingent ends included), coupled exactly by a minimum cut within a node budget - A compact, versioned, CRC-32-checked byte encoding of timelines and profiles without allocation, and optional serde support (feature serde) - Borrowed search scratch for small onboard stacks (SearchScratch) - A bridge example that checks a schedule with the windows of temporal-control's dispatcher, see examples/stn_bridge.rs - Brute-force oracles for every check, compared in property tests See docs/design.md for the semantics of each check. Usage Features Without alloc, the crate needs no allocator: timelines, state timelines and plans use storage::Fixed and storage::FixedPlan, and it builds for bare-metal targets such as thumbv7em-none-eabihf (checked in CI).
connector-routing: connector-routing Global connector routing: many orthogonal connectors at once with bend, length and crossing costs, negotiated congestion and rip-up and reroute. The crate routes connectors around rectangular obstacles, as diagram editors, schematic tools and cable-plan generators need: optimal single routes, many routes negotiating channel capacity, crossing reduction, and a final placement that separates shared stretches, plus hyperedges (Steiner trees for nets with more than two ports) and any-angle routing through sleeves or poly-lines for when the lines need not be orthogonal. All geometry is exact integer arithmetic, so results are reproducible and free of floating-point robustness issues; the crate is no_std with alloc. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. The drawing above is the output of cargo run --example svg. Scope Orthogonal routing: - Exact geometry, routing graph, orthogonal visibility graph (Wybrow, Marriott and Stuckey 2009) with a routing frame and port stubs, incremental updates for added, moved and removed obstacles and ports - Single connector: A* over (vertex, heading) with an exact free-space bend estimate; weighted and exact lexicographic length/bend objectives; checked against brute force on the unit grid - 1-bend visibility graph search (Marriott, Stuckey and Wybrow 2014), opt-in: tests show it is not exact in general, so the OVG search is the default - Global routing: PathFinder negotiated congestion over channel capacities, rip-up and reroute, crossing penalties, deterministic net order - Reports of the connectors a scene change invalidates or may improve - Path ordering in shared channels, required crossings, crossing reduction, crossing points of finished routes (for drawing hops) - Nudging: scan-line separation constraints (exported as data) solved exactly as difference constraints with water-filling, no LP; or VPSC projection of desired positions - Pipeline of arXiv 2309.01671: port assignment, visibility or channel routing graph, routing, crossing reduction, ordering, constrained or full nudging (boxes move and grow) - Hyperedges (Wybrow et al. 2012): Steiner trees by both heuristics with segment-shifting improvement, nudged like connectors - Pareto fronts over length, bends and crossings (feature multi-objective, via multiobjective-search) Any-angle routing: - Sleeve routing (arXiv 2605.17498): exact constrained Delaunay triangulation, dual-graph Dijkstra, funnel algorithm, vertex-cover batching, exits along walls between touching obstacles - Incremental poly-line routing (Wybrow et al. 2005): visibility and invisibility graphs, rerouting reports, hidden-region pruning, segment, angle and crossing penalties See docs/design.md for the models, the deviations from the papers that testing found, and the paper table. Example Performance On 192 boxes and 300 connectors (cargo bench --bench routing): the visibility graph has about 9,500 vertices and builds in 7 ms, global routing takes about 0.9 s, nudging 0.3 s, and the whole pipeline 1.3 s.
pddl: A PDDL 3.1 parser, strongly typed A parser for the Planning Domain Definition Language version 3.1, written in Rust. Crate documentation is available on docs.rs/pddl. The domain/problem types can be used independently of the parser; the parser is however enabled by default via the parser crate feature. To disable the parser and its dependencies, use Documentation comments are assembled from the PDDL papers and nergmada/planning-wiki. Editor Support pddl-lsp is a language server built on this crate. It works in VS Code, Neovim, Vim, Helix, Emacs, Sublime Text and other editors that speak the Language Server Protocol. It reports every syntax error in a file plus unknown names and wrong argument counts, and checks problems against their domain across files. It also provides hover, go to definition, references, rename, completion, signature help and formatting. Then set up your editor as described in the pddl-lsp README. For VS Code, use the extension in editors/vscode, which bundles the server compiled to WebAssembly. The parser exposes what the server builds on: pddl::syntax gives the position of every atom, list and comment, and pddl::parsers::check reports every error in a file rather than only the first. Compile-time Checked PDDL The macros feature checks PDDL while your crate compiles and turns syntax errors into compile errors. It needs Rust 1.88. The macros come from pddl-macros; see its README for all of them. The types and the parser live in pddl-core, which pddl re-exports, so that pddl-macros can use the parser without a dependency cycle. Depend on pddl, not on pddl-core. Usage Example See tests/briefcase_world.rs for the full example. Parsing a Single Problem Parsing a File with Multiple Domains and Problems PDDL files often contain multiple (define ...) blocks — domains and problems in any order. Use PddlFile to parse them all at once: Grounding to SAS+ The sas-plus feature grounds a domain and problem into a sas-plus task in Fast Downward's output.sas format, without leaving Rust: Every reachable fluent atom becomes a binary variable. Fast Downward's translator instead merges mutually exclusive atoms into multi-valued variables. The grounder supports STRIPS with typing, negative preconditions, equality, universal and existential preconditions, conditional effects and action costs. It rejects other constructs with an error instead of dropping them. See the sas_plus module docs. Validating Plans pddl-validate, a separate crate in this repository, checks plans against a domain and problem, independently of any planner, and explains the first step that fails in the style of VAL's repair advice. See its README for the supported PDDL levels. Caveat Emptor At this point the parser supports all domain and problem definition elements required to fully describe a PDDL 3.1 environment. However, since types and enum variants are named closely to the underlying BNF descriptions (see below), they may be a bit unwieldy to use still. Supported Elements Parsers were implemented based on the BNF elements listed in the paper: > "Complete BNF description of PDDL 3.1 (completely corrected)", > _Daniel L. Kovacs_ See ELEMENTS.md for a graph of BNF elements.
pddl-validate: pddl-validate An independent plan validator for PDDL: a second opinion next to VAL, with precise, machine-readable diagnostics. It is part of the pddl-rs workspace and depends only on the pddl syntax tree. It implements the validation semantics itself and shares no grounding or search code with any planner, so it does not share their bugs either. Scope A plan that uses a construct outside the supported levels is reported as Unsupported, never as valid. So are continuous change whose rate reads a changing fluent, over all conditions that are not linear in time, derived predicates in temporal plans, preferences, constraints, object fluents, PDDL 1.2 :extends and :timeless, requirement flags the parser does not know, and derived predicates that depend on their own negation. Numbers Values are f64, as the pddl parser stores them. Comparisons treat a and b as equal when |a - b| holds for any pair. A comparison that reads a fluent without a value, divides by zero or overflows is unknown, and conditions follow three-valued (Kleene) logic: (or (p) (> (f) 0)) holds when (p) does, and (and (q) (> (f) 0)) fails on (q) when (q) is false. A precondition or goal that stays unknown makes the plan invalid, as does an effect or when condition that reads an undefined value. A derived predicate whose rule is unknown is not derived; a metric whose value is undefined leaves the plan valid, without a value. A nullary total-cost without an initial value starts at 0, as in Fast Downward. Updates of one fluent in one step add up when all are increase or decrease; any other combination is a conflict. In a metric, total-time is the number of steps. Report::metric returns the metric's value for a valid plan. Temporal plans A temporal plan times every step and gives each durative action its duration, as VAL reads it: 0.000: (drive r1 base hill) 2.000. A durative action splits into a start and an end event; events at the same time form a happening. In each happening, every at start and at end condition, duration constraint and precondition is checked in the state before it, and then all effects apply at once. Between happenings, continuous effects change fluents linearly, and the over all conditions of the running actions must hold on the whole open interval: the validator checks them at every root of their comparisons and between them, which is exact for linear change. Two events that interfere (one changes what the other reads or changes) must be at least epsilon apart, 0.01 by default as in VAL (Validator::with_epsilon); an action's own start and end never interfere. Timed initial literals are events too. An untimed plan for a temporal domain runs at times 1, 2, 3, and so on; total-time is the makespan. PDDL+ Processes run while their precondition holds and add their #t rates to those of the running durative actions; events fire as soon as their precondition holds, all enabled ones together, and then the validator checks again, so events cascade (at most 1000 rounds at one time, else EventCascade). Between plan happenings, the validator ends each stretch of fixed dynamics at the first root of a process or event precondition where one switches, so the switching times are exact for linear change. Rates that read changing fluents, as in (increase (speed) (* #t 9.8)) with (decrease (height) (* #t (speed))), are nonlinear and Unsupported. Processes and events run until the plan's last step; the :time requirement is accepted. Diagnostics Validation stops at the first violation, as VAL's does. The Violation names: - the step, numbered from 1 as VAL counts, with its line in the plan file; - what fails: an unknown action or object, a wrong number of arguments, an object of the wrong type, an unsatisfied precondition or an unmet goal, an undefined fluent, a division by zero, an overflow, conflicting updates, a missing timestamp or duration, a duration constraint, an at start or at end condition, an over all condition with the time it fails, or interference with another event; - for a condition, the most specific part to blame (Unmet): the first failing conjunct or forall instance, every alternative of an or or exists, or a comparison with the values of both sides; - a repair hint in the style of VAL's "Plan Repair Advice". The report also traces each step's added and deleted atoms and updated fluents, with their values before and after. A domain or problem with an undeclared type, predicate, object or variable, or a symbol applied to the wrong number of arguments, is rejected with a ModelError before any plan runs. VAL is more lenient there.
search-core: search-core Common traits for heuristic search and planning: path costs, heuristics, goal tests and search budgets. Search algorithm crates use these traits as bounds, and users implement them once for their problem: a heuristic, goal test or budget written against search-core works with every algorithm that accepts it, whichever crate provides the algorithm. The crate is no_std, has no dependencies, and keeps to small abstractions that are useful across many search algorithms. Besides the plain unsigned integers, it ships the exact cost types Decimal (fixed point) and Lexicographic (a tie-breaking pair) and a checked f64 cost, plus the arbitrary-precision BigUint and BigInt for exact arithmetic over costs, so that an algorithm generic over C: Cost never rounds unless the caller picks a float cost. Overview Search interface Costs CostExt, WideMul and ExactArith are separate from Cost, so a custom cost type only implements the capabilities the algorithms it is used with ask for. Implement Cost for your own type to use it with any algorithm generic over C: Cost. Out of scope The crate defines no search algorithms and no problem representation. Successor generation (graphs, MDPs), search statistics and limit types, and Pareto dominance differ too much between algorithms to share, so they stay in the crates that implement the algorithms. MIGRATION.md shows how existing search crates map their own traits onto this one. Example An algorithm states the capabilities it needs as trait bounds; callers pass any implementation: Features With default-features = false, the crate needs neither std nor alloc.
sas-plus: sas-plus SAS+ / finite-domain planning tasks for Rust, compatible with Fast Downward's translator. Part of the planning and search crates; see also this crate's overview page. What is SAS+? SAS stands for Simplified Action Structures (Bäckström & Klein, 1991). The + is the extension by Bäckström & Nebel (1995, *Complexity Results for SAS+ Planning*): preconditions and goals may leave variables *undefined*, so they are partial states. A SAS+ task has: - finite-domain state variables instead of Boolean facts, e.g. ball1 ∈ {at rooma, at roomb, carry left, carry right}; - operators with preconditions, effects and a cost; - a complete initial state and a partial goal. Because the variables capture mutual exclusion directly, many heuristics (pattern databases, merge-and-shrink, cost partitioning) are defined on SAS+ rather than on STRIPS. Fast Downward calls its version the *finite-domain representation* (FDR): SAS+ plus conditional effects and axioms. Who this is for - Authors of planning heuristics and search algorithms who want one plain, validated task model to build on, with Fast Downward's translator output as a source of real benchmark domains. - Researchers who need ground truth while developing a heuristic: perfect_heuristic and the seeded random tasks turn admissibility checks into ordinary property tests. - Teams that plan on embedded or robotic hardware: the task model, projections and transition systems are no_std with alloc and have no required dependencies. - Anyone who wants ready-made heuristics rather than the building blocks should look at planning-heuristics, merge-and-shrink and cost-partition; for search over a Task, see heuristic-search, symbolic-search and decoupled-search. Usage Ground PDDL with Fast Downward's translator, then load the result in Rust: To try both steps with Docker and Task, run task ground:load. It grounds a fixture with the aibasel/downward image and loads the result with examples/load.rs. Pass DOMAIN=... PROBLEM=... to ground your own PDDL (paths inside the repository). What's in it - fdr: reader and writer for output.sas (file version 3). - Faithful to the format: mutex groups, conditional effects, axioms, and fact names are all kept. - Writes back byte-for-byte what it reads. - Parse errors carry line numbers. - to_task() converts to a Task, keeping conditional effects and axioms. - Metric 0 means unit costs, exactly as in Fast Downward's search. - Task, Operator, Effect, Axiom, Fact, State, with validation, applicability and plan checking. Effects may have conditions, and derived variables are computed by layered axioms with Fast Downward's semantics. - LabeledTransitionSystem and the Abstraction trait, the common interface for abstraction heuristics such as projections, merge-and-shrink, and cost partitioning over them. - Projection: the pattern-database abstraction. Derived variables are left out of patterns, and conditional effects whose conditions lie outside the pattern may or may not fire, so projections stay admissible. - CausalGraph: arcs from preconditions and effect conditions to effects, between co-occurring effects, and from axiom conditions to derived variables. - Test oracles: Task::perfect_heuristic() (exact h*) and random::random_task. Features - fdr (default): the output.sas reader and writer. - random (default): the random task generator. - serde: Serialize and Deserialize for the task model, transition systems, the causal graph and SasFile. Use default-features = false if you only need the task model. Fixtures - tests/fixtures/translated/: real Fast Downward translator output for nine problems, from the VHPOP and Potoroo corpora plus three written for this repo. It covers unit costs, action costs, conditional effects and derived predicates. Every file round-trips byte for byte, and the small tasks are checked against their known optima. The folder includes GPL-2.0 / Apache-2.0 test inputs and is excluded from the published crate. - tests/fixtures/: small hand-encoded files, including a minimal axiom (derived-variable) example.
